questions.q: What is the strategy pattern?
questions.explain: Each delivery method is a strategy with the same available and feeKobo methods. The checkout uses whichever the customer picked.
options: A plan for how a team releases software
A family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the code that uses them can pick one at run time without knowing how it works
A way to create objects of the right class
A way to notify many objects of an event

questions.q: In one shippingFeeKobo function, a "free over ₦50,000" line meant for standard delivery also made express free. Why does moving each method into its own strategy prevent this?
questions.explain: In the shared function, every line above a method's branch applies to it. Separate strategies have no shared lines to leak through.
options: Each method's rules live only in its own object, so a rule written for standard cannot reach express
TypeScript checks strategies for business mistakes

questions.q: The mobile app sends the method id "sameday" instead of "same-day". What should strategyFor do?
questions.explain: The old return 150_000 at the end of the if chain hid the typo. Unknown input is a bug to surface, not a case to guess.
options: Throw a clear "unknown shipping method" error, so the bug in the app is found instead of charging the wrong price

questions.q: Who should choose which strategy is used?
questions.explain: The code that uses a strategy only calls it. Keeping the choice outside is what makes strategies interchangeable and testable.
options: Something outside the code that uses it: the customer's choice, the configuration, or the data (such as the customer's tier)

questions.q: When is a strategy best written as a plain function type instead of an object with methods?
questions.explain: A function is the smallest possible strategy. The shipping strategies are objects because each has an id, an availability rule and a fee rule.
options: When it is a single calculation, such as (order) => number; the object form pays off when each strategy has several related rules and an id
When there are more than ten strategies

questions.q: Same-day delivery is only offered before 14:00 Lagos time. Why does available(order, now) take the time as a parameter?
questions.explain: The clock is part of the outside world. Passing it in keeps the rule pure and testable, as in earlier lessons.
options: Because Date does not work inside objects
So tests can check 10:30 and 15:00 deterministically, on any day and in any time zone
To make the strategy a singleton
Because strategies cannot read the clock

questions.q: In the observer pattern, what does the publisher know about its observers?
questions.explain: That ignorance is the point: new reactions are added by subscribing, and the checkout does not change.
options: The name and code of each one
Nothing beyond the shape of the event: it publishes what happened, and whoever subscribed reacts
The order in which they were written

questions.q: Why does OrderPlacedTopic.publish use Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all?
questions.explain: With allSettled, a failing analytics observer is reported by name while the e-mail and warehouse observers still complete.
options: Promise.all rejects as soon as one observer fails, hiding the others' results; allSettled waits for every observer and reports each failure
Promise.all runs observers one at a time

questions.q: Which reaction to a new order should not be an observer that may fail independently?
questions.explain: If stock is not reduced atomically with saving the order, two customers can buy the last item. It is a rule of the use case and must succeed or fail with it.
options: Reducing stock for the items ordered
Posting to the sales team's chat

questions.q: Why can "refuse the order if the account is blocked" not be an observer of order.placed?
questions.explain: An event says "this happened" in the past tense. Anything with a veto must run before that is true.
options: Observers react to something that already happened; by the time they run the order exists, so they cannot prevent it. Checks that may refuse belong inside the use case, before the order is made
Blocked accounts cannot place orders anyway

questions.q: The order is saved, and the process crashes before the in-memory event reaches the warehouse observer. What is the standard fix for events that must not be lost?
questions.explain: An in-memory event only exists in one process's memory. Storing it atomically with the order means it is delivered after a restart.
options: Write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order, and deliver it from there (or use a durable queue)
Publish the event before saving the order

questions.q: The loyalty observer assumes the e-mail observer has already run. Why is this fragile?
questions.explain: Promise.allSettled starts all observers together. If one step truly depends on another, that is a sequence inside one handler or the use case, not two observers.
options: It is not fragile; observers always run in the order they were subscribed
Observers should be independent of each other; the order can change when subscriptions move, handlers run concurrently, or a bus is swapped

questions.q: Why does subscribe return a function?
questions.explain: A topic holds a reference to every observer. Unsubscribing releases it, which is how long-running servers avoid leaking listeners.
options: It unsubscribes the observer; without it, observers attached by short-lived objects stay referenced forever (a memory leak) and keep reacting

questions.q: What does the command pattern do?
questions.explain: Once "set rice to ₦7,650" is an object, a history can execute it, keep it, undo it and write down who did it.
options: It runs shell commands from Node
It turns an action into an object that holds what is needed to carry it out (and often undo it), so actions can be recorded, undone, queued and audited
It passes requests along a chain

questions.q: When should changePrice record the previous price for undo?
questions.explain: A command created in the morning and run in the afternoon must undo to the afternoon's price. Capturing at creation would restore a stale value.
options: When the command object is created
When it executes, because the price may have changed between creating the command and running it
It should not; undo should read an audit log

questions.q: A batch command runs A, then B, then C. In which order must it undo them?
questions.explain: Later steps may depend on earlier ones (B may change what A set). Undoing in reverse is the only order that is always correct.

questions.q: What is the job of CommandHistory (the invoker)?
questions.explain: Because it only uses the Command interface, the same history works for price changes, deactivations and any future command.
options: To know how prices are stored
To run commands, keep them for undo and write the audit trail, without knowing what any command does inside
To send commands over the network

questions.q: Why must a command sent through a job queue be plain data rather than an object with methods?
questions.explain: After JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(command)), execute is undefined. So the data says what, and the worker's handler says how.
options: The queue stores text (usually JSON), and functions, closures and class methods do not survive serialisation; the worker needs a handler that knows how to carry out each command type
Methods are slower to call on a worker

questions.q: Queues deliver messages at least once. What does that require of a job handler such as "send invoice e-mail"?
questions.explain: After a worker crash the same message can be delivered again. Idempotent handlers turn "at least once" into "effectively once".
options: It must be idempotent: handling the same command twice must not send two e-mails or charge twice, for example by recording which commands were already handled
It must run faster than the queue's timeout
It must delete the queue after running

questions.q: Why does the worker validate each queued message with parseJob before handling it, even though the web server wrote it?
questions.explain: The rejected DeleteAllOrders message shows why: without a check, the worker would trust whatever arrives.
options: A message from a queue is input from outside the program: it may come from an older version, a bug, or an attacker, and TypeScript types do not exist at run time

questions.q: What is a chain of responsibility?
questions.explain: Web middleware is this pattern: logging, authentication and authorization are links in front of every route.
options: A list of people responsible for a service
A request passed along a sequence of handlers, where each one either handles it completely or does its part and passes it on
A way to create objects step by step

questions.q: Why must the error-handling middleware be the first (outermost) link?
questions.explain: Each middleware wraps everything after it, like an onion. The outermost layer sees every error on the way out.
options: It can only catch errors thrown by links that run inside it; placed later, errors from earlier links escape

questions.q: Should a rate limiter run before or after authentication?
questions.explain: If the limiter runs after authentication, a request with a wrong token is rejected with 401 before it is ever counted, so guessing is unlimited.
options: After, so only logged-in users are limited
Usually before, so failed login attempts are limited too, which stops password guessing

questions.q: What does it mean when a middleware short-circuits?
questions.explain: authenticate short-circuits with 401 when there is no valid token: the export handler is never reached.
options: It returns a response without calling next, so the remaining links and the handler never run

questions.q: A middleware accidentally calls next() twice. What can happen, and how does the lesson's chain respond?
questions.explain: A guard in the composer turns a dangerous, silent bug into an immediate error during development.
options: Nothing; the second call is ignored by JavaScript
The rest of the chain and the handler run twice (a refund could be issued twice); the lesson's chain throws "next() called twice" instead

questions.q: In the refund approval chain (support up to ₦5,000, manager up to ₦100,000, finance up to ₦1,000,000), what happens to a request for ₦5,000,000?
questions.explain: A well-built chain always gives exactly one answer, including an explicit "no" at the end of the chain.
options: It passes along the whole chain and gets the answer "nobody can approve", instead of disappearing

questions.q: With @zudojs/middleware's createPipeline and the default settings, what happens when the handler throws?
questions.explain: The default error mode is "capture", so callers check outcome.success. "throw" and "continue" are the other modes.
options: The error propagates to the caller as an exception
The run ends and the result is { success: false, error, … }; the error is captured, not thrown
The error is silently ignored and success is true

questions.q: A function picks between two tax rates with one if, and the rates have not changed in five years. Should it become a strategy?
questions.explain: Use the pattern when the symptom is real: a switch that grows with every campaign. Two stable branches are clearest as they are.
options: Yes, every if should be a strategy
No. Patterns move control flow somewhere less visible; that price is worth paying only when the rules really grow or vary
Yes, but only if written as classes
No, because strategies cannot hold numbers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The free-delivery line runs before the express branch, so big express orders are free. The misspelled method falls through to the default instead of failing.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Local time is UTC+1. At 9 UTC it is 10:00: same-day is offered. At 13 UTC it is 14:00: too late. At 23 UTC it is 00:00, and 0 is less than 14, so same-day is offered at midnight, while 0 is not at least 20, so night delivery is not. The rule "before 14:00" silently includes the small hours: exactly the kind of edge a test at fixed times reveals.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all rejects with the first failure. allSettled waits for all three and reports each outcome, which is what an event topic needs.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both observers see event 1. After stop(), only the second observer remains, so event 2 adds just 20.

questions.q: This command captures the previous price when it is created. What does this print?
questions.explain: Undo restores the value captured at creation (850000), not the 900000 that was current when the command ran. Capture the previous state in execute.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A batch executes in order and undoes in reverse. [...steps] copies the array so that reverse does not change the original.
options: do A, do B, do C, undo A, undo B, undo C
do A, do B, do C, undo C, undo B, undo A
do C, do B, do A, undo A, undo B, undo C
do A, undo A, do B, undo B, do C, undo C

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON keeps only own data properties. The method lives on the prototype and the class identity is lost, so a queued command must be plain data with a handler on the worker side.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first middleware is outermost: it starts first and finishes last. console.log runs after the whole chain, so "handler" is printed first on the line.
options: handler errors before, errors after, auth before, auth after
handler errors before, auth before, auth after, errors after
handler auth before, errors before, errors after, auth after
errors before, auth before, handler, auth after, errors after

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a token, auth returns 401 and never calls next, so the handler runs only for the second request.

questions.q: The error middleware forgot await. What does this print?
questions.explain: return next() returns the rejected promise without waiting for it, so the try block has already finished when it rejects. Only return await next() lets catch see the error.
options:
escaped: db down
escaped: db down

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Exactly 500,000 is within support's limit. One kobo more goes to the manager. Above the manager's limit, the chain ends with an explicit "nobody".

questions.q: Write taxFor(countryId) that returns a strategy from the list below and throws new Error("no tax rule for " + id) for an unknown id, then add a KE strategy (16% VAT, Math.round). The program should print 75 160 then no tax rule for ZA.
questions.explain: A new country is a new strategy in the list, and an unknown id fails loudly instead of silently using another country's rate.

questions.q: Write a Topic class with subscribe(fn) (returns an unsubscribe function) and async publish(value), which runs every subscriber, waits for all of them, and returns the number that failed. The program should print 1 [ 'email ORD-1', 'ship ORD-1' ], then 0.
questions.explain: One failing subscriber is counted, not allowed to stop the others. After unsubscribing it, the next publish has no failures.

questions.q: Write changeStock(stock, sku, qty), a command whose execute records the current quantity and sets the new one, and whose undo restores the recorded quantity. The program should print 3 then 12.
questions.explain: Capturing the previous value in execute makes undo return to 12, the value just before the command ran, not the 10 that was there when it was created.

questions.q: Write History with run(command, user) (execute, remember, audit "user: description") and undo(user) (undo the last command, audit "user: undo description", return false if there is nothing to undo). The program should print 1, false, and the audit list shown in the starter comment.
questions.explain: The history only uses the Command interface. It keeps the undo stack and the audit trail for any kind of command.
questions.expected:
1
false
[ 'musa: double price', 'ngozi: undo double price' ]

questions.q: Write parseJob(text) that returns a JobCommand only if the JSON is an object with type: "SendReceipt" and a string orderId; otherwise undefined. The program should print SendReceipt ORD-9, undefined, undefined.
questions.explain: The worker trusts nothing it reads from the queue: a wrong field type or an unknown command type is rejected before any handler runs.

questions.q: Write chain(middlewares, handler): it returns a function of ctx that calls the first middleware with ctx and a next that runs the rest, ending with the handler. The program should print [ 'log in', 'auth ok', 'handler', 'log out' ].
questions.explain: Each next runs the following link, and the last link's next runs the handler. The outermost middleware finishes last, which is why "log out" comes at the end.

questions.q: Write requireRole(role), a middleware that calls next() only when ctx.user?.role === role, and otherwise returns { status: 403 } without calling it. The program should print 403 200.
questions.explain: A middleware factory takes configuration (the role) and returns the link. It short-circuits for the wrong role, so the handler never runs for support staff.

questions.q: Build a refund approval chain with a function approver(name, limitKobo, next?) returning a function of the amount: the first approver whose limit covers the amount answers with its name; past the last one, the answer is "nobody". Use support (500000), manager (10000000) and finance (100000000). The program should print support manager finance nobody.
questions.explain: Each link either handles the request or passes it on, and the end of the chain gives an explicit answer. Changing a limit or adding a level changes the chain in one place.
